skills.title: Syntactic Complexity
skills.description: Ability to construct varied, complex sentences (subordination, embedding, nominalization) to convey nuanced relationships between ideas.

levels.criteria: Very short, simple SVO sentences; additive flow via simple coordinators.
examples: I went to the store. I bought milk. I came home.
The cat is black. It is big. I like it.

levels.criteria: Uses a wider variety of coordinating conjunctions (e.g., but, so) to connect simple ideas.
examples: I wanted to go, but it was raining, so I stayed inside.
We finished the project, and we were happy with the results.

levels.criteria: Begins to use simple subordination (because, when); application may be formulaic.
examples: I was late because the train was delayed.
She cried when she heard the news.
rubricHints: Presence of simple subordinating conjunctions (e.g., because, when)

levels.criteria: Functional, consistent use of dependent clauses to add context and detail.
examples: Since the meeting was cancelled, we went to lunch early.
I decided to go to the park even though it was cloudy.

levels.criteria: Good mix of simple, compound, and complex sentences; varied structure.
examples: The report, which was released last week, includes several key findings we should discuss.
Although the plan was rejected, we proposed an alternative that was accepted.

levels.criteria: Frequent embedded clauses; increased information density.
examples: The dog that chased the ball, which was red, ran into the street.
I think the decision we made, though difficult, was the right one.

levels.criteria: Regular multi‑clause sentences; controls hierarchical relationships across ideas.
examples: The committee’s recommendation, responding to the unexpected shortfall, was tabled for review.
The findings, though preliminary, strongly indicate the new treatment’s advantage.
rubricHints: High frequency of embeddings and participial phrases

levels.criteria: Employs nominalizations for abstraction and formal register.
examples: The realization of the project’s complexity led to a reevaluation of the timeline.
The development of this policy is a functional necessity.

levels.criteria: Mastery of varied clause types; shifts forms strategically for rhetorical effect.
examples: Why did the decision, ostensibly made to increase efficiency, reduce morale?
Consider the implications: adopting this method could save millions.
rubricHints: High variety of main clause types (declarative, interrogative, imperative)

levels.criteria: Sophisticated structural mastery: nested clauses, strategic passives, nominalizations for precise discourse.
examples: The proposed policy, predicated on careful macroeconomic analysis, should be given immediate consideration.
Although early results were inconclusive, subsequent rigorous analysis provided definitive evidence.
rubricHints: Consistently complex syntax for communicative goals

skills.title: Lexical Sophistication
skills.description: Breadth and depth of vocabulary—precision, variety, domain specificity, and effective figurative/abstract usage.

levels.criteria: Very small, high‑frequency vocabulary; heavy repetition.
examples: The house is big. It’s a good house. I like the house.
I like the stuff. It’s good. I want it now.

levels.criteria: Functional but basic vocabulary; avoids some repetition.
examples: The building was large and impressive. We saw many things inside.
It seems like a good idea and might be helpful.

levels.criteria: Introduces simple synonyms to reduce repetition.
examples: The plan was good, and the approach seemed sound.
The structure was tall, and the design was impressive.

levels.criteria: Solid general‑purpose vocabulary with some descriptive range.
examples: The conference was quite engaging, and I learned a great deal.
The proposal is sound, though I have reservations.

levels.criteria: Introduces domain‑specific terms appropriate to context.
examples: We analyzed the dataset to identify anomalies.
The system’s extensibility is a key advantage.

levels.criteria: Prioritizes precise word choice; avoids vague generalities.
examples: A dispassionate assessment supported the conclusion.
Her meticulous planning improved reliability.

levels.criteria: Effective figurative language and analogy.
examples: We need to get to the heart of the issue.
This project is the backbone of our roadmap.

levels.criteria: Comfortable with abstract and conceptual lexicon.
examples: The confluence of these factors shifted the outcome.
We must consider long‑term sustainability.

levels.criteria: Consistently sophisticated and infrequent vocabulary; nuanced register.
examples: The dichotomy between theory and practice persists.
A congenial framework for subsequent iterations emerged.

levels.criteria: Mastery: precise, domain‑appropriate, and rhetorically impactful vocabulary.
examples: This confluence precipitated a seismic shift in market equilibrium.
Our nascent initiative burgeoned into a robust methodology.
rubricHints: Expert use of infrequent and domain terms

skills.title: Discourse Coherence
skills.description: Logical organization and semantic unity across utterances; effective use of cohesive devices and information flow.

levels.criteria: Disjointed ideas with no explicit links; listener must infer relationships.
examples: I was tired. The movie was good. I ate popcorn.
My dog is small. She likes to play. I went for a walk.

levels.criteria: Simple sequencing in time; basic chronological order.
examples: I woke up. Then I went to work. After that, I came home.
First we met, and then we reviewed the notes.

levels.criteria: Introduces simple logical links (so, because, but).
examples: I was tired, so I went to bed.
The project was hard, but we finished on time.

levels.criteria: Consistent anaphora and referential clarity.
examples: I like my new car. It is reliable and it saves gas.
Our team worked hard. They delivered ahead of schedule.

levels.criteria: Functional transitional phrases to guide the listener.
examples: In addition, this approach reduces cost.
For example, we sold fewer units in Q1.
rubricHints: Presence of discourse markers (e.g., in addition, for example)

levels.criteria: Signals complex semantic relations (concession, contrast, exemplification).
examples: Nonetheless, the long‑term strategy remains sound.
On the other hand, adoption has been slower than expected.

levels.criteria: Clear macro‑structure (intro/body/conclusion); framed segments.
examples: First, I’ll outline the problem; then the solution; finally, the timeline.
Our argument proceeds in three steps: hypothesis, evidence, and implications.

levels.criteria: Coherence at sentence and paragraph level with multiple threads.
examples: Our initial hypothesis was challenged; specifically, rising input costs altered viability.
Efficiency is one issue; additionally, scalability affects long‑term success.
rubricHints: High density and variety of cohesive devices

levels.criteria: Strategic management of given/new information to reduce cognitive load.
examples: This challenge, as discussed, stems from outdated data.
These results—already noted—support a revised approach.

levels.criteria: Flawless logical cohesion throughout a multi‑layered argument or narrative.
examples: While the data suggests growth, countervailing behaviors temper our forecast; therefore, we proceed cautiously.
First and foremost, reallocate resources; once done, the path forward is clear.

skills.title: Rhetorical Effectiveness
skills.description: Strategic language use (logos, ethos, pathos) to influence outcomes via argumentation, evidence, and rhetorical moves.

levels.criteria: Descriptive/narrative only; no clear persuasive intent.
examples: The policy changed. People were upset.
It’s a phone. It works for me.

levels.criteria: Simple assertion without justification.
examples: We should adopt this software. It’s the best.
The project is important. We should prioritize it.

levels.criteria: Basic justification with a single reason (because…).
examples: We should do this because it saves time.
It’s a bad idea because it’s too expensive.

levels.criteria: Introduces explicit evidence or references.
examples: The report shows adoption is faster.
According to the data, this reduces cost.

levels.criteria: Clear thesis and logical progression from claim to evidence.
examples: Our system is inefficient; adopting X will address bottlenecks.
The team struggles; a new strategy can improve morale.

levels.criteria: Begins to use ethos (credibility) and pathos (emotion).
examples: As a veteran engineer, I’ve seen this approach succeed.
This decision affects local families; we must consider them.
rubricHints: Personal expertise markers or emotional appeals

levels.criteria: Uses refutation and/or concession to address counterpoints.
examples: Some may argue it’s costly, but long‑term benefits outweigh the initial spend.
While competitors focus on short‑term gains, we prioritize sustainability.

levels.criteria: Employs complex moves (rhetorical questions, analogies, pointed examples).
examples: If speed is our goal, why add steps?
It’s like fixing a leak by turning on the faucet.

levels.criteria: Strategic framing to shape audience perception.
examples: Invest now to avoid catastrophic failure later.
We’re not selling a product; we’re offering a blueprint for success.

levels.criteria: Rhetorical mastery: multi‑faceted argument with ethos, pathos, logos in concert.
examples: While short‑term costs rise, the data demonstrates superior long‑term returns, benefiting all stakeholders.
We cannot disregard community needs; our shared future demands this path.

skills.title: Lexical Fluency (Filler Reduction)
skills.description: Smooth, confident delivery with minimal disfluencies; strategic repetition/pauses for effect rather than hesitation.

levels.criteria: Heavily disfluent; frequent fillers and repetitions.
examples: I, uh, think the, um, report was, like, good.
So, I, uhm, went to the store and, uh, I got stuff.

levels.criteria: Frequent fillers; message still recoverable but effortful.
examples: The new, um, system is, uh, complex.
We can, uh, start next week.

levels.criteria: Moderate fillers; appear when searching for words or transitioning.
examples: I believe we should, um, wait for the data.
The plan is, uh, solid overall.

levels.criteria: Occasional fillers; typically under cognitive load.
examples: The implications are, um, significant.
We need to, uh, consider all variables.

levels.criteria: Minimal fillers; hesitations brief and non‑disruptive.
examples: I propose a phased rollout with real‑time feedback.
The analysis results are conclusive.

levels.criteria: Repetition used intentionally for emphasis.
examples: This is a crucial—crucial—step.
I am certain—absolutely certain—this will work.

levels.criteria: Intentional unfilled pauses to aid processing and emphasis.
examples: Our priority is quality … then speed.
The solution, as I see it, is simple.

levels.criteria: Highly fluid speech; near‑zero disfluencies.
examples: The implications are clear; the path forward is unequivocal.
Let’s proceed with confidence and clarity.

levels.criteria: Strategic pacing; varies rate and pauses to maintain attention.
examples: This. Is. Not. Optional.
We’re ready … the technology is prepared … now we execute.

levels.criteria: Effortless fluency; entirely free of non‑purposeful hesitations.
examples: The committee’s unanimous decision advances our trajectory.
Effective communication is clear, concise, and intentional.
